topics.title: Tricky scales: reading between the marks
topics.intro: On real scales most marks have no number. Work out what each mark is worth first, then count. If the arrow is between two marks, make a sensible estimate.
topics.teach: Explain how you worked out what each mark is worth on a scale numbered 0, 100, 200 with 5 jumps between the numbers.
topics.talk: Read the kitchen scales or a measuring jug together. Ask {him} what each little mark is worth.

visual.caption: 5 jumps from 0 to 10, so each mark is worth 2. The arrow is 2 marks after 30: 34.
Each mark is worth 10. This arrow is halfway between 30 and 40: about 35.

topics.title: Using 2, 5 and 10 facts to find new ones
topics.intro: If you know your 2, 5 and 10 times tables, you can work out lots more. 5 × 12 is 5 × 10 and 5 × 2. 5 × 8 is half of 10 × 8!
topics.teach: Explain how knowing 10 × 14 = 140 helps you work out 5 × 14.
topics.talk: Ask {him}: “If 6 × 5 = 30, what is 12 × 5? How do you know?”

topics.title: Balancing number sentences
topics.intro: The = sign means “is the same as”, like a balance. Both sides must make the same amount. Look at how the numbers change, and you often don’t need to work out the total.
topics.teach: Explain how you know 45 + 38 = 40 + 43 without adding.
topics.talk: Ask {him} to make up a balancing puzzle, like 10 + 6 = 12 + ?

visual.caption: 29 + 17 = 15 + 4 + ?  Both sides make 46. 15 + 4 = 19, which is 10 less than 29, so ? is 10 more than 17: 27.

topics.title: Thinking problems: totals and differences
topics.intro: Draw it! A bar for each person, with the extra bit marked, shows what to do. Take away the extra, and the rest splits into equal bars.
topics.teach: Explain how drawing bars helps you solve: “Together Jack and Sam have £14. Jack has £2 more than Sam. How much does Sam have?”
topics.talk: Share 14 sweets so one person has 2 more. Ask {him} how {she} worked it out.

visual.caption: Take away Jack’s extra £2: £14 − £2 = £12. Two equal bars: £12 ÷ 2 = £6. Sam has £6 and Jack has £8.

topics.title: Which is more? Multi-step problems
topics.intro: Some problems need two or three steps. Work out each amount first, then compare. Don’t trust your first guess: more packets does not always mean more biscuits!
topics.teach: Explain which has more biscuits, 4 packets of 5 or 3 packets of 10, and how you know.
topics.talk: At the shop, ask {him} which is cheaper: one big packet or two small ones.

visual.caption: 4 packets of 5 = 20 biscuits. 3 packets of 10 = 30 biscuits. Fewer packets, but more biscuits!

topics.title: Time to 5 minutes
topics.intro: Every number on the clock is 5 minutes for the long hand. When the long hand is on the right side, it is “past” the hour; on the left side it is “to” the next hour.
topics.talk: Ask {him} the time on an analogue clock at different times of day, and how long until the next meal.

visual.caption: 3:40. The long hand is on 8: 4 jumps of 5 before 12, so it is twenty to 4.

topics.title: Same and different: comparing shapes
topics.intro: Mathematicians compare shapes: what is the same, and what is different? Count faces, edges and vertices, check the sides, and look for lines of symmetry.
topics.teach: Explain what is the same and what is different about a cube and a cuboid.
topics.talk: Find two boxes at home. Ask {him} what is the same and what is different about them.

visual.caption: A cube: 6 square faces, 12 edges, 8 vertices.
A cuboid: also 6 faces, 12 edges, 8 vertices, but its faces can be rectangles.

items.prompt: A cube and a cuboid. What is the SAME about them?

options.text: They both have 6 faces, 12 edges and 8 vertices
All of their edges are exactly the same length
options.feedback: Only the cube’s edges are all the same length. A cuboid can be long and thin.

options.text: All of their faces are squares, like a dice
options.feedback: A cube’s faces are all squares, but a cuboid can have rectangle faces.

options.text: They both have 8 faces, 12 edges and 6 vertices
options.feedback: Count again: faces and vertices are swapped. Both have 6 faces and 8 vertices.

items.explain: Count them: both have 6 faces, 12 edges and 8 vertices. What is different is their size and shape: a cube’s edges are all equal.

visual.caption: Cube: 6 faces, 12 edges, 8 vertices. All edges equal.
Cuboid: 6 faces, 12 edges, 8 vertices. Faces can be rectangles.

items.prompt: What is DIFFERENT about a cube and a cuboid?

options.text: A cube’s faces are all squares; a cuboid’s can be rectangles
A cuboid has more faces and edges than a cube does
options.feedback: Both have 6 faces and 12 edges.

options.text: A cube has more vertices, because it is taller
options.feedback: Both have 8 vertices: 4 on the top and 4 on the bottom.

items.explain: They have the same number of faces, edges and vertices, but different dimensions: every edge of a cube is the same length.

visual.caption: Cube: 6 faces, 12 edges, 8 vertices. All edges equal.
Cuboid: 6 faces, 12 edges, 8 vertices. Faces can be rectangles.

items.prompt: How many edges does a cuboid have?
items.explain: The same as a cube: 4 round the top, 4 round the bottom and 4 going up.

visual.caption: 4 edges round the top, 4 round the bottom, 4 going up: 12.

items.prompt: How many vertices (corners) does a cuboid have?
items.explain: The same as a cube: 4 on the top and 4 on the bottom.

visual.caption: 4 vertices on the top and 4 on the bottom: 8.

items.prompt: Turbo says: “A cube is a special kind of cuboid.” Is he right?

options.text: Yes: it is a cuboid whose faces are all squares
No: a cuboid’s faces must be rectangles
options.feedback: A square is a special rectangle, with all 4 sides equal. So a cube still counts as a cuboid.

options.text: No: a cube has more edges
options.feedback: Both have 12 edges.

items.explain: A cuboid has 6 rectangle faces. A square is a special rectangle, so a cube (6 square faces) is a special cuboid.

visual.caption: Cube: 6 faces, 12 edges, 8 vertices. All edges equal.
Cuboid: 6 faces, 12 edges, 8 vertices. Faces can be rectangles.

items.prompt: What do a square and a rectangle BOTH have?

options.text: 4 sides and 4 right angles
4 equal sides
options.feedback: Only the square has 4 equal sides. A rectangle has 2 long sides and 2 short sides.

options.text: 4 lines of symmetry
options.feedback: A square has 4 lines of symmetry, but a rectangle (that is not a square) has only 2.

items.explain: Both have 4 sides and 4 right angles. A square’s sides are all equal; a rectangle’s are not.

visual.caption: Dashed red lines are lines of symmetry: 4 for the square, 2 for the rectangle.

items.prompt: How many lines of symmetry does a rectangle have (one that is not a square)?
items.explain: One down the middle and one across the middle. The diagonals are not lines of symmetry: fold along one and the corners do not match.

feedback.4: A square has 4. Fold a rectangle along a diagonal and the corners do not meet.

visual.caption: Down the middle and across the middle: 2 lines of symmetry.

items.prompt: Which shape has exactly ONE line of symmetry?

options.text: a kite
a square
options.feedback: A square has 4 lines of symmetry.

options.text: a rectangle
options.feedback: A rectangle has 2 lines of symmetry.

options.text: a circle
options.feedback: A circle has lots and lots: any line through the middle.

items.explain: A kite folds exactly in half only down the middle, from its top point to its bottom point.

visual.caption: The kite has 1 line of symmetry. The rectangle has 2.

items.prompt: An isosceles triangle (2 equal sides) and a kite. What is the SAME about them?

options.text: They both have exactly one line of symmetry
They both have exactly 4 sides and 4 vertices
options.feedback: The kite has 4 sides and 4 vertices, but a triangle has 3 of each.

options.text: They both have exactly 2 lines of symmetry
options.feedback: Each one folds in half only down the middle: 1 line of symmetry each.

items.explain: Each one folds exactly in half down the middle, and nowhere else: one line of symmetry each.

visual.caption: Each has exactly 1 line of symmetry, straight down the middle.

items.prompt: Which has only ONE line of symmetry: a semicircle or a circle?

options.text: a semicircle
a circle
options.feedback: A circle can be folded in half along any line through its middle: it has lots of lines of symmetry.

options.text: They both have one
options.feedback: A circle has lots of lines of symmetry. Only the semicircle has just one.

items.explain: A semicircle only folds in half down the middle. A circle folds in half along any line through its centre.

visual.caption: A semicircle has 1 line of symmetry. A circle has lots: any line through its centre.

items.prompt: How many lines of symmetry does the capital letter A have?
items.explain: One, straight down the middle. The two sloping sides match when you fold it.

visual.caption: Fold the A down the middle and the two sides match.

items.prompt: The letter A has exactly one line of symmetry. Which of these letters ALSO has exactly one?

options.text: T
H
options.feedback: H has 2 lines of symmetry: one down and one across.

options.text: F
options.feedback: F has no line of symmetry: it does not match when folded.

options.text: N
options.feedback: N has no line of symmetry. It looks the same upside down, but that is not a fold.

items.explain: T folds in half straight down the middle, just like A.

visual.caption: T has 1 line of symmetry, like A. H has 2. F has none.

items.prompt: Which triangle has exactly ONE line of symmetry?

options.text: a triangle with exactly 2 equal sides
a triangle with all 3 sides equal
options.feedback: A triangle with 3 equal sides (equilateral) has 3 lines of symmetry.

options.text: a triangle with no sides the same length
options.feedback: A triangle with no equal sides has no line of symmetry.

items.explain: A triangle with exactly 2 equal sides is called isosceles. It folds in half down the middle, between its 2 equal sides.

visual.caption: Isosceles: 1 line. Equilateral: 3 lines. A triangle with no equal sides: none.

items.prompt: Which shape has MORE than one line of symmetry?

options.text: a rectangle
a kite
options.feedback: A kite has just 1 line of symmetry.

options.text: a semicircle
options.feedback: A semicircle has just 1 line of symmetry.

options.text: an isosceles triangle
options.feedback: An isosceles triangle has just 1 line of symmetry.

items.explain: A rectangle has 2: down the middle and across the middle. The others have just 1.

visual.caption: The rectangle has 2 lines of symmetry; the kite has 1.

items.prompt: How many faces does a square-based pyramid have?
items.explain: 1 square on the bottom and 4 triangles: 5 faces.

visual.caption: 1 square face on the bottom and 4 triangle faces: 5.

items.prompt: How many faces does a triangular prism have?
items.explain: 2 triangles at the ends and 3 rectangles: 5 faces.

visual.caption: 2 triangle faces at the ends and 3 rectangle faces: 5.

items.prompt: A square-based pyramid and a triangular prism both have 5 faces. What else is the SAME?

options.text: All their faces are flat
They both have 8 edges
options.feedback: The pyramid has 8 edges, but the prism has 9.

options.text: They both have 6 vertices
options.feedback: The prism has 6 vertices, but the pyramid has 5.

items.explain: Both have only flat faces. But the pyramid has 8 edges and 5 vertices, and the prism has 9 edges and 6 vertices.

visual.caption: Square-based pyramid: 5 faces, 8 edges, 5 vertices.
Triangular prism: 5 faces, 9 edges, 6 vertices.

items.prompt: What is DIFFERENT about a square-based pyramid and a triangular prism?

options.text: Only the pyramid comes to a point (an apex)
Only the prism has triangle faces on it
options.feedback: The pyramid has 4 triangle faces too.

options.text: Only the prism has a curved surface
options.feedback: Neither has a curved surface: all their faces are flat.

options.text: Only the pyramid has rectangle faces
options.feedback: The prism has 3 rectangle faces. The pyramid has a square and 4 triangles.

items.explain: A pyramid’s triangle faces meet at a point (an apex) at the top. A prism is the same shape all the way along: a triangle at each end, joined by rectangles.

visual.caption: Square-based pyramid: 5 faces, 8 edges, 5 vertices.
Triangular prism: 5 faces, 9 edges, 6 vertices.

items.prompt: What do a cone and a cylinder BOTH have?

options.text: A circle face and a curved surface
Two circle faces
options.feedback: Only the cylinder has two circle faces. A cone has one.

options.text: A point at the top (an apex)
options.feedback: Only the cone has an apex.

items.explain: A cone has 1 circle face, a curved surface and a point. A cylinder has 2 circle faces and a curved surface.

visual.caption: Cone: 1 circle face, a curved surface and a point (apex).
Cylinder: 2 circle faces and a curved surface.

items.prompt: What is DIFFERENT about a cone and a cylinder?

options.text: A cone has 1 circle face; a cylinder has 2
A cylinder has no curved surface at all
options.feedback: A cylinder has a curved surface all the way round, like a tin of beans.

options.text: A cone cannot roll, but a cylinder can
options.feedback: Both can roll on their curved surface.

items.explain: Both have a curved surface. The cone has 1 circle face and comes to a point; the cylinder has a circle face at each end.

visual.caption: Cone: 1 circle face, a curved surface and a point (apex).
Cylinder: 2 circle faces and a curved surface.

items.prompt: What do a sphere and a cylinder BOTH have?

options.text: A curved surface, so they can roll
Flat circle faces at both ends
options.feedback: A cylinder has 2 flat circle faces, but a sphere has none: it is curved all over.

options.text: Vertices where their edges meet
options.feedback: Neither has a vertex (corner).

items.explain: Both have a curved surface. A sphere is curved all over; a cylinder also has 2 flat circle faces.

visual.caption: Sphere: one curved surface, no flat faces.
Cylinder: 2 circle faces and a curved surface.

items.prompt: A cube and a square-based pyramid both have a square face. What is DIFFERENT?

options.text: A cube has 6 faces; the pyramid has 5
The pyramid has more vertices
options.feedback: The pyramid has 5 vertices and the cube has 8: the pyramid has fewer.

options.text: The cube has triangle faces
options.feedback: A cube’s faces are all squares. The pyramid has the triangle faces.

items.explain: A cube has 6 square faces, 12 edges and 8 vertices. A square-based pyramid has 5 faces (1 square, 4 triangles), 8 edges and 5 vertices.

visual.caption: Cube: 6 faces, 12 edges, 8 vertices.
Square-based pyramid: 5 faces, 8 edges, 5 vertices.
